summary: Subjects and verbs must agree in number and person. A singular subject requires a singular verb; a plural subject requires a plural verb. The key challenge is identifying the true subject when intervening phrases are present.
key_rules: Singular subjects take singular verbs: 'The dog runs'
Plural subjects take plural verbs: 'The dogs run'
Intervening phrases between subject and verb do not affect agreement
Collective nouns (team, committee) take singular verbs in standard usage

worked_examples.question: Identify the error:
worked_examples.wrong: The quality of the reports were poor.
worked_examples.correct: The quality of the reports was poor.
worked_examples.why: Subject is 'quality' (singular), not 'reports'. 'of the reports' is an intervening phrase.

worked_examples.question: Choose the correct form:
worked_examples.wrong: Neither the manager nor the employees was present.
worked_examples.correct: Neither the manager nor the employees were present.
worked_examples.why: With 'neither...nor', verb agrees with the closer subject: 'employees' (plural).

common_mistakes: Agreeing with the nearest noun instead of the true subject
Errors with neither/nor and either/or constructions
exam_tips: Cross out prepositional phrases to isolate the true subject
For neither/nor and either/or, verb agrees with the subject closest to it

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence:

options.A: The group of students are working hard.
options.B: The group of students is working hard.
options.C: The groups of student are working hard.
options.D: The group of students were working hard.

quiz.explanation: 'Group' is the singular subject; 'of students' is an intervening phrase. Singular subject takes singular verb 'is'.

quiz.question: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?

options.A: Neither the teacher nor the students was ready.
options.B: Neither the teacher nor the students were ready.
options.C: Neither the teachers nor the student were ready.
options.D: Neither the teacher nor the student are ready.

quiz.explanation: With neither/nor, the verb agrees with the closer subject: 'students' (plural) → 'were'.

quiz.question: Select the correctly constructed sentence:

options.A: Each of the candidates have submitted their forms.
options.B: Each of the candidates has submitted their forms.
options.C: Each of the candidate have submitted their form.
options.D: Each of the candidates have submitted his forms.

quiz.explanation: 'Each' is always singular regardless of the following phrase. 'Each...has' is correct.

summary: Parallelism requires that grammatically equal ideas be expressed in the same grammatical form. When items appear in a list or comparison, they must all use the same part of speech and structure.
key_rules: Items in a list must use the same grammatical form
Correlative conjunctions (both/and, either/or, not only/but also) require parallel elements

worked_examples.question: Fix the parallelism error:
worked_examples.wrong: She enjoys reading, writing, and to swim.
worked_examples.correct: She enjoys reading, writing, and swimming.
worked_examples.why: 'to swim' is an infinitive; it must be a gerund like the other items: 'swimming'.

worked_examples.question: Identify the error in this comparison:
worked_examples.wrong: Running is more enjoyable than to cycle.
worked_examples.correct: Running is more enjoyable than cycling.
worked_examples.why: Both sides of a comparison must use the same form. 'Running' is a gerund, so 'cycling' must match.

common_mistakes: Mixing infinitives (to run) with gerunds (running) in the same list
Forgetting to repeat articles or prepositions in formal parallel structures
exam_tips: Scan sentences for lists and comparisons first — they are the most common parallelism test site
Identify the first item's form, then verify all other items match

quiz.question: Which sentence is correctly parallel?

options.A: He likes to run, swimming, and cycling.
options.B: He likes running, to swim, and cycling.
options.C: He likes running, swimming, and cycling.
options.D: He likes to run, to swim, and cycles.

quiz.explanation: Option C uses all gerunds (-ing forms): running, swimming, cycling. All items are grammatically identical.

quiz.question: Identify the parallel error:

options.A: The report was thorough, accurate, and well-written.
options.B: The report was thorough, accurate, and written well.
options.C: The report was thorough, accurately done, and well-written.
options.D: The report was thorough, accurate, and concise.

quiz.explanation: 'Thorough' and 'well-written' are adjectives; 'accurately done' is an adverb+verb phrase. It breaks the adjective pattern.
